query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: By partially substituting tungsten with a ductility‐promoting element such as vanadium in the NbMoTaW refractory HEA, a dual-phase microstructure with nanometer‐scale, coherent V-rich precipitates will form within the BCC matrix, thereby improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance without sacrificing high-temperature mechanical strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW that exhibits excellent high-temperature strength (up to 1600 °C) but poor room temperature ductility and uncertain irradiation behavior.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor fraction (e.g., ~5 at.%) of vanadium by partially replacing tungsten in the NbMoTaW alloy composition, followed by a controlled annealing treatment designed to precipitate fine, ductile V-rich phases.
generation.conditions: The alloy will be evaluated at room temperature for ductility and at elevated temperatures (up to 1600 °C) for mechanical strength, as well as under irradiation conditions (e.g., helium implantation to simulate fusion reactor environments).
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, coherent V-rich precipitates embedded in the BCC matrix that act as ductile secondary phases and defect sinks.
generation.mechanism: The V-rich precipitates are expected to locally soften the BCC matrix by promoting additional deformation mechanisms such as enhanced dislocation slip or even twinning, thereby increasing room temperature ductility. In addition, these precipitates provide heterogeneous interfaces that can act as sinks for irradiation-induced point defects, reducing defect accumulation and mitigating irradiation-induced amorphization and precipitation, while the overall BCC matrix preserves the excellent high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the modified alloy is predicted to have significantly improved room-temperature ductility (e.g., increased strain to failure) and reduced irradiation-induced damage (such as less amorphization or blistering) with minimal change in its high-temperature (up to 1600 °C) mechanical performance.
generation.baseline: The original NbMoTaW refractory HEA with equiatomic BCC structure, high strength at elevated temperatures, but exhibiting poor ductility at room temperature and computationally suggested irradiation resistance.
generation.boundary: The improvements are expected to hold within the temperature range from ambient to 1600 °C and under irradiation conditions comparable to helium implantation experiments; however, the stability of the dual-phase microstructure under extreme irradiation flux or prolonged high-temperature exposure remains to be determined.
generation.uncertainty: The exact volume fraction and distribution of V-rich precipitates, the kinetics of their formation during the annealing process, and any potential adverse effects on the high-temperature phase stability of the BCC matrix are not fully predictable without experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys: (1) the baseline equal-atomic NbMoTaW and (2) the modified alloy with ~5 at.% V replacing part of W. Apply identical processing and controlled annealing treatments to both. Conduct room-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or compressive tests), high-temperature (up to 1600 °C) mechanical performance evaluation, and irradiation experiments (e.g., helium implantation at controlled doses). Characterize the microstructure using TEM and XRD to confirm the formation and coherence of V-rich precipitates.
measurements: Room-temperature ductility (strain to failure, elongation measurements)
High-temperature yield strength and creep resistance measurements
Irradiation-induced damage assessment via TEM and defect density measurements
Microstructural analysis (phase distribution, precipitate size and coherency) using TEM and XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the V-modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance compared to the baseline NbMoTaW alloy, or if the high-temperature mechanical performance is compromised (e.g., significant decrease in yield strength or phase instability), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Twinning-induced strain hardening in dual-phase FeCoCrNiAl0.5 at room and cryogenic temperature

Abstract: AbstractA face-centered-cubic (fcc) oriented FeCoCrNiAl0.5 dual-phase high entropy alloy (HEA) was plastically strained in uniaxial compression at 77K and 293K and the underlying deformation mechanisms were studied. The undeformed microstructure consists of a body-centered-cubic (bcc)/B2 interdendritic network and precipitates embedded in 〈001〉-oriented fcc dendrites. In contrast to other dual-phase HEAs, at both deformation temperatures a steep rise in the stress-strain curves occurs above 23% total axial strain. As a result, the hardening rate associated saturates at the unusual high value of ~6 GPa. Analysis of the strain partitioning between fcc and bcc/B2 by digital image correlation shows that the fcc component carries the larger part of the plastic strain. Further, electron backscatter diffraction and transmission electron microscopy evidence ample fcc deformation twinning both at 77K and 293K, while slip activity only is found in the bcc/B2. These results may guide future advancements in the design of novel alloys with superior toughening characteristics.

Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Irradiation Damage Independent Deuterium Retention in WMoTaNbV

Abstract: AbstractHigh entropy alloys are a promising new class of metal alloys with outstanding radiation resistance and thermal stability. The interaction with hydrogen might, however, have desired (H storage) or undesired effects, such as hydrogen-induced embrittlement or tritium retention in the fusion reactor wall. High entropy alloy WMoTaNbV and bulk W samples were used to study the quantity of irradiation-induced trapping sites and properties of D retention by employing thermal desorption spectrometry, secondary ion mass spectrometry, and elastic recoil detection analysis. The D implantation was not found to create additional hydrogen traps in WMoTaNbV as it does in W, while 90 at% of implanted D is retained in WMoTaNbV, in contrast to 35 at% in W. Implantation created damage predicted by SRIM is 0.24 dpa in WMoTaNbV, calculated with a density of 6.044×1022 atoms/cm3. The depth of the maximum damage was 90 nm.
